0.title: Fruitful to the End
0.overview:
Our culture prizes youth. Advertising, entertainment and even churches often focus on the young. Older people can feel invisible, unwanted or a burden. Many fear ageing: the loss of health, independence, friends, purpose and memory. Retirement, which promises leisure, can bring emptiness.

Scripture sees old age very differently. Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life (Prov 16:31). The righteous still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green (Ps 92:14). God promises to carry his people from birth to old age: even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you (Isa 46:4).

This study is for those who are growing older, and for those who love and care for them. It looks honestly at the losses of ageing, and hopefully at the fruitfulness God offers in the later years, the calling to pass on the faith, and the grace to finish well.

Five units: (1) The Crown of Gray Hair; (2) The Losses of Age; (3) Purpose in the Later Years; (4) Passing On the Faith; (5) Dependence and Finishing Well.

1.title: The Crown of Gray Hair
1.overview:
Honour the aged. You shall stand up before the gray head and honor the face of an old man, and you shall fear your God: I am the LORD (Lev 19:32). In Israel, respect for the elderly was tied to the fear of God. The old were to be honoured, consulted and cared for.

A crown of glory. Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life (Prov 16:31). Old age is not something to hide or be ashamed of. A long life of faithfulness is a glory. The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendor of old men is their gray hair (Prov 20:29). Each stage of life has its own beauty.

Wisdom. Older people have seen much and learned much. Wisdom is with the aged, and understanding in length of days (Job 12:12). Not every older person is wise, but those who have walked with God for many years have wisdom the young need.

God carries his people. Listen to me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been borne by me from before your birth, carried from the womb; even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you (Isa 46:3-4). The God who carried us as infants will carry us in old age. He does not abandon his people when they become weak.

Fruitful in old age. The righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They are planted in the house of the LORD; they flourish in the courts of our God. They still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green (Ps 92:12-14). Spiritual fruitfulness does not depend on physical strength.
1.theology:
Against ageism: A culture that values people for their productivity or appearance will devalue the old. Scripture values people because they bear God's image, at every age.

Life as a gift: Long life is often presented in Scripture as a blessing (Exod 20:12; Ps 91:16). Each additional year is a gift of God's grace.

The church as a family: In a healthy church, old and young need each other. The old give wisdom and stability; the young give energy and fresh vision.
1.examples:
Then: When Rehoboam became king, he rejected the counsel of the old men who had served his father Solomon, and listened instead to the young men he had grown up with. His foolish decision split the kingdom (1 Kgs 12:6-16). Despising the wisdom of the old has consequences.

Now: A church makes a point of including older members in its life: asking them to share testimonies, mentor younger believers and pray for the church. Younger members find their faith strengthened. Older members feel valued rather than sidelined.

A simple test: How does your church honour its older members?

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall stand up before the gray head and honor the face of an old man, and you shall fear your God: I am the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God commands his people to rise before the gray head and honour the face of the old, and to fear God. Respect for the elderly is not merely good manners; it is part of reverence for God. How we treat the old reflects how we view God.

verseByVerse.quote: Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Gray hair is a crown of glory, gained in a righteous life. A long life lived in faithfulness to God is honourable. Age is not a loss to hide but a crown to wear.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen to me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been borne by me from before your birth, carried from the womb; even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God has carried Israel from birth and will carry them to old age and gray hairs. He made them, and he will bear and save them. Unlike idols, which must be carried, God carries his people. This promise holds for every believer in old age.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They are planted in the house of the LORD; they flourish in the courts of our God. They still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green, to declare that the LORD is upright; he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The righteous are like flourishing palm trees and cedars, planted in God's house. They still bear fruit in old age and remain full of life. Their lives declare that the LORD is upright and that there is no unrighteousness in him. Old age can be a testimony to God's faithfulness.

1.reflection:
How does Scripture's view of old age differ from our culture's?

What wisdom have you received from older believers?

How does Isaiah 46:3-4 encourage those growing older?

What does it mean to "bear fruit in old age"?

2.title: The Losses of Age
2.overview:
Ageing brings real losses, and Scripture does not hide them.

The body declines. Ecclesiastes 12 describes old age in vivid poetry. Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years draw near of which you will say, "I have no pleasure in them" (Eccl 12:1). It speaks of trembling keepers of the house, grinders that cease and windows that grow dim, images often taken as the hands, the teeth and the eyes, and of the fear of heights. The body weakens.

Loss of strength and role. Barzillai, at eighty, declined King David's invitation to live at court. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? (2 Sam 19:35). He felt his age and knew his limits.

Fear of abandonment. Do not cast me off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength is spent (Ps 71:9). Many older people fear being forgotten, by family, by society, even by God.

Loss of loved ones. The longer we live, the more people we lose: spouses, friends, siblings, sometimes children. Grief becomes a frequent companion. Loneliness can be one of the hardest burdens of old age.

Loss of memory. Some face dementia, which can take away memory and personality. This is a hard road, for the person and for their family. Yet God does not forget those who forget him. He knows and holds them still.

Inward renewal. So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16). The body declines, but the soul can grow. Many believers grow most in faith, patience and love in their last years.
2.theology:
Lament is allowed: The losses of age are real, and believers may grieve them honestly before God, as the psalmists did.

God remembers: For those with dementia, salvation does not depend on remembering God, but on God remembering them. The Lord knows those who are his (2 Tim 2:19).

Resurrection hope: The decline of the body is not the end. Believers await bodies raised imperishable, glorious and powerful (1 Cor 15:42-44).
2.examples:
Then: In Psalm 71, an old believer prays for help against enemies and the fear of abandonment. Yet he resolves, But I will hope continually and will praise you yet more and more (Ps 71:14). Old age did not end his praise; it deepened it.

Now: A widow in her eighties has outlived most of her friends and feels lonely. Her church arranges regular visits, and a young family adopts her as an honorary grandmother. She begins praying for them daily. Her loneliness eases, and her prayers become a gift to them.

A simple test: Is there an older person you know who is lonely? How could you visit or include them?

verseByVerse.quote: Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years draw near of which you will say, "I have no pleasure in them"; before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars are darkened and the clouds return after the rain, in the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bent, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those who look through the windows are dimmed, and the doors on the street are shut—when the sound of the grinding is low, and one rises up at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song are brought low— they are afraid also of what is high, and terrors are in the way; the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper drags itself along, and desire fails, because man is going to his eternal home, and the mourners go about the streets— before the silver cord is snapped, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is shattered at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern, and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Preacher urges the young to remember their Creator before old age comes. He describes the decline of the body in poetic images: darkening lights, trembling limbs, failing senses. Finally the silver cord snaps, the dust returns to the earth and the spirit to God who gave it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not cast me off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength is spent. For my enemies speak concerning me; those who watch for my life consult together and say, "God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is none to deliver him." O God, be not far from me; O my God, make haste to help me! May my accusers be put to shame and consumed; with scorn and disgrace may they be covered who seek my hurt. But I will hope continually and will praise you yet more and more. My mouth will tell of your righteous acts, of your deeds of salvation all the day, for their number is past my knowledge. With the mighty deeds of the Lord GOD I will come; I will remind them of your righteousness, yours alone. O God, from my youth you have taught me, and I still proclaim your wondrous deeds. So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation, your power to all those to come. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: An aged believer pleads not to be cast off in old age. Enemies take advantage of his weakness. Yet he hopes continually and praises more and more. He longs to declare God's power to the next generation, even in gray hairs.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he went on with the king to the Jordan, to escort him over the Jordan. Barzillai was a very aged man, eighty years old. He had provided the king with food while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man. And the king said to Barzillai, "Come over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem." But Barzillai said to the king, "How many years have I still to live, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem? I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king? Your servant will go a little way over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward? Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him go over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you." And the king answered, "Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me I will do for you." Then all the people went over the Jordan, and the king went over. And the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own home. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Barzillai, at eighty, had supported David in exile. David invited him to Jerusalem, but Barzillai declined, aware of his failing senses and wishing to die in his own town. He asked David to honour his son instead. Barzillai faced his age with honesty and grace.

verseByVerse.quote: So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day. For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison, as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The outer self wastes away, but the inner self is renewed day by day. Present afflictions are light and momentary compared with eternal glory. The losses of age can be faced with hope, because what is unseen is eternal.

2.reflection:
Which losses of ageing do you fear most?

How does Psalm 71 show faith in old age?

What does it mean that "our inner self is being renewed day by day"?

How could you care for an older person facing loss?

3.title: Purpose in the Later Years
3.overview:
No retirement from the Christian life. Our culture often presents retirement as an extended holiday. There is nothing wrong with rest and enjoyment after years of work. But Scripture knows no retirement from serving God. The later years can be among the most fruitful.

Caleb. At eighty-five, Caleb said, I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming. So now give me this hill country (Josh 14:11-12). Few will have Caleb's strength, but all can have his spirit.

Simeon and Anna. When the infant Jesus was brought to the temple, two elderly believers recognised him. Simeon had waited his whole life for the Messiah. Anna, a widow of great age, did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day (Luke 2:37). She spoke of the child to all who were waiting for redemption. God gave these two old people the privilege of welcoming his Son.

Older men and women. Paul gave specific instructions for older believers. Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness. Older women are to be reverent and to teach what is good, and so train the young women (Titus 2:2-4). Older believers have a ministry of example and teaching.

Ministries of the older. Older believers can pray (perhaps the greatest ministry of all), mentor younger Christians, show hospitality, visit the sick, serve in church, volunteer in the community and share the gospel. Time, experience and wisdom are gifts to be used.

Stewarding resources. Many older people have savings and possessions. Scripture calls for generosity and wise planning, including leaving an inheritance and supporting the work of the gospel (Prov 13:22).
3.theology:
Vocation lasts: A person's calling is not only their paid work. Every believer is called to serve God and others throughout life. Retirement changes the shape of that calling, not its existence.

Rest and work: Rest in later years is a gift. But a life of only leisure is not satisfying. Purpose and service bring joy at every age.

Prayer ministry: Older believers who cannot do much else can pray. Their prayers are powerful (Jas 5:16). Some of the church's greatest work is done by elderly saints on their knees.
3.examples:
Then: Moses was eighty when God called him to lead Israel out of Egypt (Exod 7:7). His most important work began when most people would have stopped working.

Now: A retired engineer decides to use his skills and time for his church: helping with maintenance, mentoring young men, leading a weekly prayer meeting and volunteering at a local charity. He says these are the most rewarding years of his life.

A simple test: If you are retired or nearing retirement, how will you use these years for God?

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. And Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, "You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God in Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me. I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought him word again as it was in my heart. But my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt; yet I wholly followed the LORD my God. And Moses swore on that day, saying, 'Surely the land on which your foot has trodden shall be an inheritance for you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God.' And now, behold, the LORD has kept me alive, just as he said, these forty-five years since the time that the LORD spoke this word to Moses, while Israel walked in the wilderness. And now, behold, I am this day eighty-five years old. I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming. So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Caleb reminded Joshua of God's promise forty-five years earlier. At eighty-five, he asked for the hill country, where giants lived. He trusted God to help him drive them out. Age did not dim his faith or his eagerness to claim God's promises.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ. And he came in the Spirit into the temple, and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he took him up in his arms and blessed God and said, "Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel." And his father and his mother marveled at what was said about him. And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, "Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed." And there was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin, and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day. And coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Simeon, righteous and devout, had been promised that he would see the Messiah. He took the baby Jesus in his arms and praised God. Anna, a widow of great age, worshipped constantly and spoke of the child to all who were waiting. Two elderly saints were among the first to welcome Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness. Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good, and so train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul tells Titus to teach older men to be sober, dignified and sound in faith, and older women to be reverent and to train younger women. Older believers are not on the sidelines. They are teachers and examples for the next generation.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They are planted in the house of the LORD; they flourish in the courts of our God. They still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green, to declare that the LORD is upright; he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The righteous still bear fruit in old age. They are full of sap and green. They declare that the LORD is upright. The later years are a time to bear fruit, not to fade away.

3.reflection:
How does Scripture's view of later life differ from popular ideas of retirement?

What can you learn from Caleb, Simeon and Anna?

What ministries could older believers in your church take on?

How are you using, or planning to use, your later years for God?

4.title: Passing On the Faith
4.overview:
Telling the next generation. So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation, your power to all those to come (Ps 71:18). One of the great callings of old age is to pass on faith in God to the young.

The pattern of Scripture. Psalm 78 describes the task: We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD, and his might, and the wonders that he has done... so that they should set their hope in God (Ps 78:4, 7). Faith is passed from generation to generation through telling God's works.

Grandparents. Paul reminded Timothy of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well (2 Tim 1:5). A grandmother's faith shaped a future church leader. Grandparents have a unique opportunity to pray for, teach and encourage their grandchildren.

Telling your story. Older believers have stories of God's faithfulness: answered prayers, hard seasons survived, lessons learned. These stories are precious to the young. Writing them down or telling them aloud is a gift.

Mentoring. Older Christians can mentor younger ones in faith, marriage, parenting, work and suffering. Younger believers often long for this, but may not know how to ask.

Praying for the young. Older believers who cannot do much else can pray faithfully for children, grandchildren and the young people of the church. These prayers may bear fruit long after they have died.
4.theology:
Covenant faithfulness across generations: God's covenant promises extend for you and for your children (Acts 2:39), and his steadfast love is to a thousand generations (Deut 7:9) of those who love him. Faith is not inherited automatically, but God often works through families.

When children have strayed: Many older believers grieve children or grandchildren who have left the faith. They can keep praying, keep loving, and trust God, who is able to save. The prodigal son came home.

Legacy: The greatest legacy is not money or possessions but faith passed on. A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children (Prov 13:22), and the best inheritance is knowledge of God.
4.examples:
Then: In Deuteronomy, Moses commanded parents to teach God's words to their children when sitting at home, walking along the road, lying down and rising up (Deut 6:7). Faith was to be woven into everyday life across the generations.

Now: A grandfather begins writing letters to each of his grandchildren, telling them how he came to faith, how God helped him through hard times and what he prays for them. Years after his death, one grandson reads the letters and is moved to return to Christ.

A simple test: What story of God's faithfulness could you tell to a younger believer this month?

verseByVerse.quote: O God, from my youth you have taught me, and I still proclaim your wondrous deeds. So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation, your power to all those to come. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The psalmist has known God since youth and still proclaims his wonders. He asks God not to forsake him in old age until he has told the next generation of God's power. Old age has a purpose: to pass on the knowledge of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Give ear, O my people, to my teaching; incline your ears to the words of my mouth! I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings from of old, things that we have heard and known, that our fathers have told us. We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD, and his might, and the wonders that he has done. He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers to teach to their children, that the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn, and arise and tell them to their children, so that they should set their hope in God and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments; and that they should not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation, a generation whose heart was not steadfast, whose spirit was not faithful to God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The psalmist resolves not to hide God's deeds from the children, but to tell the coming generation. God commanded fathers to teach their children, so that they would set their hope in God and not be like their stubborn ancestors. Faith is passed on through faithful telling.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God whom I serve, as did my ancestors, with a clear conscience, as I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day. As I remember your tears, I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy. I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well. For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands, for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul remembers Timothy's sincere faith, which first lived in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. A grandmother and mother shaped a young man who would become a pastor. Paul urges Timothy to fan into flame God's gift. Generations of faith build on one another.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might. And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise. You shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's words are to be on the heart and taught diligently to children, talked about at home and on the road, at bedtime and in the morning. Faith is passed on not only through formal teaching but through everyday conversation.

4.reflection:
Who passed on the faith to you? How?

What stories of God's faithfulness could you share with younger believers?

How can grandparents influence their grandchildren's faith?

Who could you mentor or pray for regularly?

5.title: Dependence and Finishing Well
5.overview:
Learning dependence. Jesus told Peter, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go (John 21:18). Many older people must learn to depend on others for things they once did themselves. This can be humbling and hard. But it can also teach grace, gratitude and trust.

Caring for the elderly. Scripture commands families to care for their older members. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God (1 Tim 5:4). Paul's words are strong: if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith (1 Tim 5:8). The church also has a responsibility to care for those without family (Jas 1:27).

Care homes and difficult decisions. Sometimes families cannot provide the care an elderly relative needs, and a care home is the most loving option. This is not abandonment if the family continues to visit, love and advocate for them.

Finishing well. Paul, near the end of his life, could say, I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith (2 Tim 4:7). Finishing well means persevering in faith to the end, not drifting or becoming bitter in old age. Many Bible characters started well and finished badly. Older believers need grace to finish well.

Numbering our days. So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom (Ps 90:12). Older believers can prepare for death practically and spiritually, putting affairs in order and their hearts at peace. The Death, Dying and Heaven study explores this further.
5.theology:
Dependence and dignity: Needing help does not diminish a person's dignity. Christ himself was carried as a baby and helped to carry his cross. Dependence is part of being human.

Bitterness in old age: Some people grow bitter, critical and fearful as they age. Others grow gentler, more grateful and more trusting. The difference is often the habits of a lifetime, and the grace of God.

The goal: Old age is preparation for glory. The believer's best days are not behind but ahead.
5.examples:
Then: Solomon began well but, when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods (1 Kgs 11:4). His old age was a sad decline. By contrast, Paul finished faithfully. Starting well is not enough; we must finish well.

Now: A woman in her nineties now lives in a care home and needs help with everything. She cannot read her Bible anymore, but she knows many psalms by heart. She recites them to the carers and thanks them for every kindness. They say she is the most grateful person they have ever looked after.

A simple test: What habits are you building now that will shape the kind of old person you become?

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go." (This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God.) And after saying this he said to him, "Follow me." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus told Peter that in old age others would dress him and carry him where he did not want to go. This pointed to the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. Then Jesus said, Follow me. Dependence and death can still be ways of following Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Honor widows who are truly widows. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God. She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day, but she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives. Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach. But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul instructs the church to honour widows who are truly in need, and families to care for their own. Showing godliness to one's own household includes repaying parents and grandparents. Neglecting to care for one's relatives is a denial of the faith.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul, near death, describes his life as a drink offering poured out. He has fought the good fight, finished the race and kept the faith. He looks forward to the crown of righteousness. Finishing well is the goal of every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty; yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away. Who considers the power of your anger, and your wrath according to the fear of you? So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Our years are seventy, or by strength eighty, full of toil and soon gone. The right response is to ask God to teach us to number our days, so that we may gain a heart of wisdom. Awareness of mortality leads to wisdom.

5.reflection:
How can dependence on others in old age become an opportunity for grace?

What responsibilities do families and churches have toward the elderly?

What does it mean to finish well?

What habits now will help you grow old with grace rather than bitterness?
